extracted.intended_audience: beginning and experienced TeX users; authors preparing high-quality technical/mathematical manuscripts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing high-quality, technically-rich manuscripts using TeX (plain TeX and user-defined formats), including typographic conventions, control-sequence usage, macro-writing, and indexing. Targets both novices (how to input files and basic constructs) and advanced users (macro definition, primitives, formats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal: produce the finest quality technical manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: With TeX the goal is to produce the finest quality: this requires more attention to detail, but you will not find it much harder to go the extra distance, and you'll be able to take special pride in the finished product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose TeX when you want high-quality, book-grade typography (especially for mathematics); simpler systems suffice for merely passable documents. Expect to invest attention to detail to achieve superior typographic results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite skills for readers/authors
rubrics_metrics.description: All that you really ought to know, before reading on, is how to get a file of text into your computer using a standard editing program. Basic computer usage is not explained here. Some previous experience with technical typing will be quite helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be able to edit files and understand basic typing; the manual assumes that and does not teach general computer use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'dangerous bend' sign to mark advanced material
rubrics_metrics.description: A special sign designates material that is for wizards only: when the symbol appears it warns of a 'dangerous bend' in the train of thought: don't read the paragraph unless you need to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/readers can ignore these advanced paragraphs on first pass; they indicate topics not needed for basic use but available for experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises: attempt before consulting answers
rubrics_metrics.description: EXERCISES are sprinkled through this manual. It is generally intended that every reader should try every exercise, except for questions in 'dangerous bend' areas. If you can't solve a problem, you can look up the answer, but try first yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exercises to internalize concepts; consult Appendix A only after attempting problems to maximize learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks: produce proper left/right quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: To produce double-quote marks with TeX type two single-quote characters of the appropriate kind (e.g., ``I understand.''). Many terminals have only a non-oriented double-quote, so you must supply oriented quotes via sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type `` and '' for opening/closing double quotes; use  (notation in manual) or control sequences like \lq and \rq when terminal lacks characters. Ensure correct oriented quotes in final typeset output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hyphen, en-dash, em-dash, and minus sign
rubrics_metrics.description: In good math books these symbols are all different: a hyphen (-), an en-dash (--), an em-dash (---), and a minus sign (- in math mode). Each has distinct uses (hyphen for compounds, en-dash for ranges, em-dash for sentence punctuation, minus sign in formulas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type - for hyphen, -- for en-dash, --- for em-dash, and use $-$ (math mode) for minus sign. Be conscientious about choosing the correct symbol for the semantic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ligatures and kerning are handled automatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain combinations of letters (ff, fi, fl, ffi, ffl, etc.) are treated as units (ligatures) and TeX can handle them by itself; TeX also kerns adjacent letters where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on TeX's automatic ligature substitution and kerning rather than manual fixes; TeX will convert sequences like -- to --- and adjust letter spacing appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix adjacent-quote spacing with \thinspace
rubrics_metrics.description: When quotes occur adjacent to each other (e.g., a single quote followed by a double quote) naive input may look wrong; the manual recommends typing '\thinspace' between them to produce the visually correct small space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting a full normal space between adjacent quotes (too large) or relying on grouping tricks; use \thinspace to get the desired small spacing: e.g. '\thinspace'' produces the correct look.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escape character (backslash) and control-sequence syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: One keyboard character is reserved as the escape character (usually backslash). Immediately after it you type a coded command (a control sequence). Control sequences come in two flavors: control words (\ followed by letters) and control symbols (\ followed by one nonletter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember that control words require a space or nonletter to end them; digits are not letters in this sense. Choose backslash as escape for consistency; use control symbols for single-character commands when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spaces after control words are ignored; use control-space to force a real space
rubrics_metrics.description: When a space comes after a control word it is ignored by TeX (not considered a real manuscript space). To insert a space after a control word type control-space (escape followed by an actual blank).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '\ ' (backslash-space) after macros when you need a visible space (e.g., '\TeX\ ignores...' to get a space after \TeX). Note other nonprinting sequences like return/tab are treated similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer high-level macros over primitives
rubrics_metrics.description: About 300 TeX control sequences are primitives (low-level atomic operations). It is generally better to use higher-level control sequences (macros) that state the desired function rather than programming with primitives repeatedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define and use macros (higher-level control sequences) for repeated tasks; reserve primitives for low-level format definition or when necessary. This reduces errors and eases future changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encapsulate formatting rules in macros (example: \exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level macros should encapsulate formatting details. The \exercise macro, for example, computes the exercise number, typesets the heading with the triangle in the left margin, leaves appropriate space or pagebreaks, prohibits pagebreak after the heading, and suppresses indentation on the following line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put layout, numbering, spacing, and other style behavior inside macros so changing presentation requires editing only the macro definition, not each instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain TeX and formats: base vs user formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX is a set of about 600 basic control sequences commonly present when TeX begins; plain TeX is only one of countless formats that can be designed on top of TeX's primitives. Appendix E contains example formats (including the manual's own format).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with plain TeX and adapt definitions gradually as you gain experience; supply or adopt formats appropriate to your document class (business letters, books, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect macro meanings with \show
rubrics_metrics.description: You can display the meaning of any control sequence while running TeX by typing \show\cs; TeX will respond with its current meaning (primitive or macro expansion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \show to debug or understand what a control sequence does (appears on terminal and in log). Helpful when distinguishing primitives from defined macros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font usage: select appropriate typefaces and limit emphasis faces
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX provides commands to switch fonts: \rm, \sl, \it, \tt, \bf. Special fonts are effective for emphasis but not for sustained reading; roman type should account for the bulk of material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bold/italic/slanted/typewriter for short emphasized stretches; avoid long passages entirely in non-roman faces. Use grouping (braces) to confine font changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use braces { } to localize font and grouping changes
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX provides curly braces to switch fonts (or other settings) inside { and } without affecting surrounding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer {\bf bold} rather than \bf ... \rm pairs where possible, to make font changes local and less error-prone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control-sequence names are case-sensitive and distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no built-in relationship between uppercase and lowercase letters in control sequence names; e.g., \pi and \Pi are different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with capitalization in macro names; define meaningful names and avoid relying on case equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX's built-in vocabulary and extensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX understands about 900 control sequences initially (primitives + plain TeX macros), and it's easy to define more. Many macros fall into few categories (math symbols, accents, formats).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the subset you need; extend TeX with user macros for custom notation; consult Appendices (B, F, E) for lists of primitives, macros, symbol tables and example formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use math mode for formulas; experience improves results
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX will automatically do most formatting of equations, but users with more experience will be able to obtain better results since there are many ways to deal with formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put mathematics between dollar signs (or display modes) and learn more advanced techniques only if necessary to refine appearance; novices need not master all details to get good results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing conventions and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Important works should contain indexes; an index is placed at the end, set in smaller type, thoroughly alphabetized. The upper-right fine print in the manual pages is a draft of intended index entries; actual scope and formatting determined later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan indexing during manuscript preparation; note that index entries may extend across several pages and may use typographic distinctions; report missing index items to the compiler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not redefine special control sequences carelessly (control-space, return/tab)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonprinting control characters like (return) and (tab) are initially set up to act like control-space; these special control sequences should probably not be redefined because you can't see the difference in a file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid redefining nonprinting control sequences that are visually indistinguishable in source, to prevent hard-to-detect bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro-based document design for easy future changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the manual is entirely described in terms of high-level control sequences, it could be printed in a radically different format simply by changing a dozen or so definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure documents so that stylistic decisions live in macro definitions and style files; this makes large-scale format changes straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent in input but not obsessive about spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX treats two or more consecutive spaces as a single space; typists taught to put two spaces after sentences needn't be consistent because TeX handles spacing rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't worry about exact number of typed spaces; learn TeX's spacing conventions and use control-space when a literal extra space is required.
